A2.text:
Aysel is a nurse at a hospital in Baku. She works the night shift, from eight in the evening to eight in the morning. She is also studying for a big exam. She wants to become a head nurse.

For two months, Aysel did not sleep much. After work, she studied all day. She had to burn the midnight oil every night. She also did overtime to cover for a sick friend.

Aysel was exhausted. She drank a lot of coffee. “I can't run on empty much longer,” she told her mother on the phone. “But the deadline for the exam is next week.”

One night, she was on call. An old man, Mr Rafael, needed his medicine. Aysel was so tired that she almost gave him the wrong pills. She stopped just in time.

Her boss, Nurse Sevda, saw her face. “Aysel, this is burnout,” she said. “Go home and call it a day. You need sleep, not coffee.”

Aysel went home and slept for twelve hours. After that, she changed her plan. She studied for three hours a day and always took a nap before her shift.

A week later, she took the exam. She passed with a high score.

Mr Rafael gave her a box of chocolates. “Now,” he said, “sleep a little more.”

B1.text:
Aysel had worked as a nurse at a hospital in Yasamal for four years, mostly on the night shift. This autumn she had a big goal: the exam to become a senior nurse. The date was fixed, and she had six weeks to prepare.

So she made a plan that looked heroic on paper. Work from eight in the evening until eight in the morning. Study from nine until three. Sleep, if possible, from three until seven. When a colleague broke her arm, Aysel even agreed to cover her shifts, which meant two extra nights of overtime every week.

For a while, it worked. She burned the midnight oil — and the midday oil too — and filled notebook after notebook. But by the fifth week, she was exhausted in a way that coffee couldn't fix. “I'm running on empty,” she admitted to her sister, “but it's only one more week.”

Then, at four in the morning, while she was on call in the cardiology ward, she prepared the medicine for Mr Rafael, a retired engineer in Room 12. Just as she was about to give it to him, she looked again at the label. It was the wrong patient's medicine.

Her heart nearly stopped. Nothing had happened — but it so easily could have.

The head nurse, Sevda, found her shaking in the staff room. She didn't shout. “This is how burnout starts,” she said quietly. “Call it a day. Go home and sleep. I'll find someone for the rest of your shift.”

Aysel slept for thirteen hours. When she woke up, she threw away her heroic plan. She studied three hours a day, stopped covering extra shifts and took a proper nap before every night at work.

She passed the exam with the third-highest score in the city.

On her next shift, Mr Rafael handed her a box of chocolates. “For the new senior nurse,” he said. “But promise me something. Eat them after you sleep.”

B2.text:
Aysel had spent four years as a nurse in a hospital in Yasamal, most of them on the night shift, and this autumn she had set herself a formidable goal: the senior nurse examination. The deadline for preparation was immovable, and she had six weeks.

The schedule she devised was magnificent on paper and catastrophic in practice. Work from eight in the evening until eight in the morning; study from nine until three; sleep, circumstances permitting, from three until seven. When a colleague fractured her wrist, Aysel volunteered to cover two of her shifts a week as well, adding a steady stream of overtime to an already impossible timetable.

For a month, sheer willpower carried her. She burned the midnight oil and most of the afternoon oil besides, filling notebook after notebook with dosages and protocols. By the fifth week, however, she was exhausted in a way no amount of coffee could touch. Her hands trembled; words slipped away mid-sentence. “I'm running on empty,” she confessed to her sister, “but it's only one more week.”

At four o'clock one morning, while on call in cardiology, she prepared the medication for Mr Rafael, a retired engineer in Room 12. With the cup already in her hand, some instinct made her glance at the label once more. The name on it belonged to another patient.

She stood frozen. Nothing had happened — but the distance between nothing and disaster had been a single glance.

Sevda, the head nurse, found her trembling in the staff room. There was no reprimand. “This is what burnout looks like at the beginning,” she said gently. “Call it a day. Go home and sleep. I'll arrange cover for the rest of your shift.”

Aysel slept for thirteen hours straight. When she woke, she discarded the magnificent schedule entirely: three focused hours of study a day, no extra shifts, and a non-negotiable nap before every night at work.

She passed the examination with the third-highest score in the city.

On her next shift, Mr Rafael presented her with a box of chocolates. “For the new senior nurse,” he said, then wagged a finger. “On one condition. You eat them after a full night's sleep.”

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is working late. And I'm a bit tired today — I worked until midnight yesterday.
Why so late?
A big deadline. The report was due this morning, so I had to burn the midnight oil.
Did you get paid for the overtime?
[laugh] No. That's not how it works in my office.
My cousin Nigar is a nurse. She works night shifts — from eight in the evening to eight in the morning.
Twelve hours at night? How does she sleep?
With black curtains and earplugs. She sleeps when everyone else is awake.
That sounds really hard on the body.
It is. After a month of nights she was completely exhausted. She told me, "I can't run on empty any more."
In England many doctors and nurses leave because of burnout. It's a big problem.
Here too. Now she does nights only one week a month.
Good. My secret for long days is a nap. Twenty minutes after lunch, and I'm a new man.
In the office?
In my car! [chuckle] With the seat back.
My dad was a baker. He started at three in the morning, every day, for thirty years.
Three in the morning! When did he finish?
At noon. Then he said, "Okay, let's call it a day," and slept all afternoon.
Honestly, that sounds better than my office.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: do you ever work or study late — and how do you stay awake?
And when do you call it a day? See you next time!
Bye for now!
